_🎯 Functional Correctness_ | _🟠 Major_ | _⚡ Quick win_

**Refresh the clock at the timer arm site.**

This refresh only covers work executed before `Loop.poll` returns. `Loop.add` calls `armTimer` without another refresh, and `armTimer` uses cached `nowFor`. If a callback or task batch runs longer than the timer duration after this update, the next duration timer is calculated from the stale snapshot and can fire immediately. Read the clock in the `.duration` branch of `armTimer` so the deadline is relative to the actual arm time.

<details>
<summary>Proposed fix</summary>

```diff
-            .duration => |d| timer.deadline = self.nowFor(timer.clock).addDuration(d),
+            .duration => |d| timer.deadline = time.now(timer.clock).addDuration(d),
```
</details>

The residual you describe is real and is discussed in the PR thread: a task batch that runs longer than a timer's duration after the refresh still computes a backdated deadline. The per-arm clock read was the first version of this PR; the maintainer chose the cache-preserving shape deliberately — the per-scan snapshot keeps duration timers armed within one tick on a shared base, so same-tick timers fire together even when a task hogs the executor. The post-wake refresh closes the observed hole (idle wake up to max_wait); the long-batch case is a known, accepted trade-off of that design.

`@dimenus`, understood. The cached clock in `LoopState.armTimer` is intentional.

A per-arm read would change same-tick timer semantics. It would remove the accepted long-task-batch trade-off, but it would also prevent duration timers in the same tick from sharing one time base.

I withdraw this finding. 🐇

This makes duration timers armed in the same tick share a common time base. A duration timer armed after a long CPU-bound task batch can be backdated, but this is an accepted trade-off. `Loop.poll` refreshes the cache after a potentially blocking backend poll to prevent timers from being backdated by the idle poll wait.

I don't think we need this flag. We should just unconditionally update now. And the `updateNow` in `checkTimers` can be then removed.

Done — the refresh is now unconditional in `poll` right after the backend call, and the `updateNow` at the top of `checkTimers` is removed, so the post-poll site is the single refresh point (plus `setTimer`). Net cost unchanged: one clock read per poll, relocated. Revalidated on this shape: 653/653, the regression test still fails on main and passes here, and the h2spec case passes 4 of 4 full-suite runs.

_🎯 Functional Correctness_ | _🟡 Minor_ | _⚡ Quick win_

**Guard the post-poll refresh for non-zero waits.**

Line 1429 runs when `should_poll` is false and when `wake_flags` causes `backend.poll` to receive `.zero`. Neither path slept, so the cached snapshot is not stale by backend wait time. The extra refresh advances `tick` and gives callbacks after a non-blocking poll a different timer base from the initial scan. This breaks the per-scan timer-base contract and contradicts the zero-timeout behavior in the PR objective.

Capture the actual timeout passed to `backend.poll` and refresh only when it is non-zero.

<details>
<summary>Proposed fix</summary>

```diff
         const should_poll = wait or self.backend.hasInflight();
         const wake_flags = self.state.wake_requested.swap(0, .acq_rel);
-        const timed_out = if (should_poll) try self.backend.poll(&self.state, if (wake_flags != 0) .zero else timeout) else false;
+        const poll_timeout: Duration = if (wake_flags != 0) .zero else timeout;
+        const timed_out = if (should_poll) try self.backend.poll(&self.state, poll_timeout) else false;

-        self.state.updateNow();
+        if (should_poll and poll_timeout.value != 0) self.state.updateNow();
```

</details>
